rationale: A wins because it separates four real reporter shapes and knows exactly where each one breaks. Its cleanest move is splitting "Glossier spent a decade selling direct. Now it says wholesale is its fastest-growing channel" from "Sephora at Kohl's gets Glossier," which creates different protagonists instead of reheating the same retail story. B is competent, but "The DTC darling that quietly became a wholesale company" overstates the facts: fastest-growing wholesale is not the same as becoming wholesale-led. That flourish is how a decent angle gets murdered by the first follow-up question.
gaps_in_A: The Kohl's angle leans on a thin premise: "what the shop-in-shop deal says about where the brand wants to sell" needs the Kohl's door count before it fully earns its own lane.
The fragrance angle says "the category Glossier is using to fill those shelves," then correctly asks for proof; keep that as a question, not a near-claim.
A could have called out that privately held/no revenue disclosure weakens every implied success story, not just the contrarian angle.
gaps_in_B: "The DTC darling that quietly became a wholesale company" is overclaiming. The update says wholesale is fastest-growing, not that Glossier has become a wholesale company.
"covering the collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" turns one company's unnumbered claim into a market obituary. That is a fake trend unless you bring outside proof.
"The prevailing belief ... is real and widely held" is not in the update. It may be true, but this exercise rewards grounded angles, not confident ambient wisdom.
B skips Sephora at Kohl's as a distinct protagonist, so it leaves a real trade-retail angle on the floor.
